strengths: Novel application of empowerment to text-based LM agents, addressing a real gap in scalable goal-agnostic evaluation; First empowerment estimator explicitly designed for language environments

Rigorous experimental validation with direct empowerment ground truth in controlled environments (Gridworld, Tower of Hanoi) showing strong alignment (Pearson r correlation plots in Figure 3), plus comprehensive ablations across agent dimensions (CoT, memory, model scale/family)

Demonstrates robustness to natural language paraphrasing of structured observations (Table 1: EELMA RMSE 0.048-0.127 vs direct estimation 0.302-0.438), indicating practical applicability despite state description variability

Practical safety relevance demonstrated through authentication case study (Figure 8) detecting power-seeking behaviors without explicit reward signals, achieving significant empowerment difference for valid vs. invalid credentials (0.365 vs -0.127 bits, p<0.001)
Strong empirical correlation with task performance across domains (r=0.91 for closed models, 0.83-0.94 for most WebArena domains), supporting empowerment as performance proxy
Comprehensive reproducibility: code available, detailed methodology in appendices E-H, explicit hyperparameters, multiple training seeds, clear algorithmic descriptions (Algorithm 1)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: EELMA primarily adapts Myers et al. (2025)'s contrastive successor representation to text embeddings via InfoNCE loss; the core algorithmic contribution is incremental rather than introducing fundamentally new methods for MI estimation in language spaces

Concerning robustness failure on realistic linguistic variation: Appendix I reveals severe degradation with natural language conversion (Hanoi: EELMA-NL achieves 0.025 bits vs ground truth 0.295 bits, only 8.5% of reference value), undermining claims of robustness despite Table 1's positive results on paraphrasing structured observations

Empowerment metric exhibits domain-dependent limitations: Shopping tasks show flat empowerment-reward relationship despite correlations elsewhere (Figure 7B); paper acknowledges empowerment fails when reasoning (not navigation) is bottleneck, suggesting bias toward exploration tasks and limited applicability as 'general-purpose' capability metric

Theoretical connection to performance relies on three unvalidated assumptions (Skill Coverage assuming uniform reward distribution, Ergodicity, Boltzmann rationality) with no empirical verification of when/whether these hold; Skill Coverage assumption particularly unrealistic for real-world task distributions

Missing key baselines and ablations: no comparison to simpler metrics (action entropy, state visitation entropy, average step count); no ablation on discount factor γ (fixed at 0.9); unclear whether EELMA's complexity yields meaningfully better performance monitoring than alternatives

Scope limitations reduce immediate applicability: tested on relatively simple environments (5×5 Gridworld, 4-disk Tower of Hanoi, web navigation with limited state space); scalability to high-dimensional observations/actions and continuous control domains unexplored; WebArena augments with synthetic LLM-generated goals not counted toward reward, raising questions about real capability coverage

Natural language handling paradox: claims robustness (Table 1) on paraphrases of structured states, but Appendix I shows drastic failures (8.5% performance) on realistic semantic variation; limited evaluation on truly open-ended text environments with high linguistic diversity

Notation and presentation issues: Equation (1) uses τ ~ Geom(1-γ) inconsistently; relationship between theoretical equations (2-3) and implementation (Eq. 7) unclear; constants C₁, C₂ in equations (5-6) undefined; negative empowerment values (Figure 8: -0.127 bits) lack clear interpretation

strengths: Novel application of empowerment to LM agents, adapting a classical concept to high-dimensional language spaces
Comprehensive experimental coverage across multiple domains (games and realistic web browsing) with extensive ablations on CoT, memory, and model factors
Scalable algorithm that enables empowerment estimation where direct calculation is intractable, using pretrained embeddings and InfoNCE
Robustness evaluation demonstrating EELMA's generalization to natural language variability better than direct estimation baselines
Detailed experimental documentation with code, prompts, and hyperparameters supporting reproducibility
Interesting case study on authentication showing empowerment can detect pivotal state transitions without explicit reward signals
weaknesses: Core empirical claim insufficiently supported: correlations in Figure 6 are moderate (r=0.70-0.91), not 'strong' as claimed; WebArena Shopping domain shows flat relationship, contradicting universality; no statistical significance testing reported

Theoretical assumptions (Skill Coverage, Ergodicity, Boltzmann Rationality) are restrictive and never empirically validated; disconnect between theory requiring uniform reward distribution and realistic sparse-reward tasks
EELMA method lacks design justification: why 2-layer MLP with 32-dim embeddings? How much does fine-tuning help vs. pretrained embeddings? InfoNCE tightness never analyzed

Absence of baseline comparisons: no comparison to task success rate (simpler and always available), other information-theoretic metrics, or alternative evaluation frameworks, making it impossible to assess relative value

Limited experimental scope: WebArena shows extremely low agent success rates (5-15%), raising data quality concerns; inconsistent model allocation across domains; direct estimation validation unavailable for realistic settings
Speculative safety application: authentication case study is somewhat tautological (valid actions lead to new states); no evidence EELMA detects genuinely unsafe power-seeking behavior

Natural language robustness claims overstated: Table 1 shows EELMA(NL) has higher RMSE than EELMA(fixed), and Figures 11-12 show substantial degradation; robustness is mainly that learned embeddings generalize, which is unsurprising
Insufficient analysis of failure modes: beyond acknowledging Shopping domain failure, no systematic investigation of when/why empowerment fails for a purportedly 'general-purpose' metric
Computational cost and practical deployment considerations completely absent; no discussion of when practitioners should use empowerment vs. simpler alternatives

strengths: Novel application of empowerment to LM agent evaluation addressing a real gap in goal-agnostic capability assessment
Rigorous theoretical framework formalizing effective empowerment with clear connection to agent capability
Comprehensive empirical validation across toy domains (ground truth validation with r>0.9) and realistic settings with multiple model families
Sound methodological approach using pretrained embeddings and variational MI estimation to handle high-dimensional text spaces
Excellent presentation, reproducibility, and extensive appendices with implementation details and task specifications
Compelling case study demonstrating detection of privileged access without explicit reward signals (authentication scenario)
Strong correlations between empowerment and performance across different ablations (CoT, memory, model size)
weaknesses: Theoretical assumptions (Skill Coverage, Ergodicity, Boltzmann rationality) are restrictive and not empirically validated, creating a gap between theory and practice
Shopping domain shows zero correlation between empowerment and reward (Figure 7B), fundamentally undermining generality claims; the 'reasoning bottleneck' explanation is insufficiently rigorous
Limited scope to text-based environments only (games and web); no robotics, visual observation spaces, or diverse modalities despite claims of general-purpose evaluation
Natural language robustness claims overstated: Appendix I shows severe degradation with NL conversion (91% loss on Hanoi domain) contradicting Table 1's robustness claims

Connection between contrastive objective convergence and mutual information (Eq. 5-6) lacks formal justification; no analysis of when learned representations might fail or sensitivity to hyperparameters (embedding dimension, temperature τ)
Missing critical comparisons to simpler baselines (trajectory length, state visit diversity, action entropy) and other goal-agnostic metrics, making it unclear if empowerment adds value
Goal-agnostic claim overstated: method still requires well-defined state spaces and depends on trajectory diversity, creating circular dependency between empowerment estimation and agent exploration

Incomplete analysis of failure modes: why do open-source models show 25% lower correlations (r=0.70 vs 0.91)? Why does Shopping domain fail specifically? When will practitioners expect empowerment to work?
Power-seeking case study demonstrates obvious behavior (successful authentication → empowerment spike) with no evidence of detecting subtle or unintended behaviors as claimed in abstract
Insufficient statistical rigor: small sample sizes in some correlations, missing confidence intervals, no significance testing for domain-wise differences

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing scalable, goal-agnostic evaluation of LM agents with solid theoretical grounding in empowerment literature
Sound technical contribution: EELMA cleverly combines dual InfoNCE objectives with language embeddings to estimate empowerment in high-dimensional text spaces
Comprehensive empirical validation: strong correlations in most settings (Gridworld/Hanoi R²=0.80-0.94, WebArena GitLab/Reddit Rs=0.83-0.94), robust to linguistic variability (Table 1)
Demonstrates practical utility: Figure 9 shows EELMA identifies pivotal actions (authentication) without manual annotation; outperforms simple diversity baselines (Table 5)
Excellent presentation with clear motivation (Figure 1), algorithm overview (Figure 2), implementation details in appendices, and honest discussion of limitations and failure modes
Thorough ablations on design choices (CoT, memory, model scale) showing empowerment consistently tracks performance across agent variations
weaknesses: Core theoretical limitation under-addressed: uniform reward assumption (Appendix A.2) required to justify empowerment-capability connection is restrictive and unrealistic; insufficient main-text discussion of when this assumption holds

Significant empirical failure modes inadequately explored: WebArena Shopping shows essentially zero correlation (r≈0.05), τ-bench retail exhibits inverted correlation when models are at floor performance, Qwen shows 40.6% jailbreaking with task-irrelevant state diversity—relegation to appendices minimizes concerns

Approximation bias undermines interpretability: negative empowerment values occur in practice (Figure 9: -0.127 bits) violating MI definition; Eq. 6's reliance on C₁-C₂≈0 is unverified for finite K, yet practitioners lack guidance on when estimates are trustworthy
Limited algorithmic novelty: EELMA combines existing components (InfoNCE, LoRA, pretrained embeddings); no comparison to alternative MI estimators or recent goal-agnostic metrics

Experimental design concerns: (1) WebArena augmentation with LLM-generated goals creates train-test mismatch; (2) causality unclear—correlations may reflect base model capability rather than empowerment driving performance; (3) statistical significance largely absent except Table 4

Insufficient guidance on practical applicability: requires collecting trajectories per agent, ~50% data stabilization reported without domain-specific analysis; failure modes suggest narrow reliability regime; design choices (LoRA, base encoder) not well-motivated in main text despite importance shown in appendices

strengths: Well-motivated problem: addresses the real need for scalable, goal-agnostic LM agent evaluation beyond expensive benchmarks
Rigorous validation in controlled settings: strong alignment between EELMA and direct empowerment estimation in Gridworld/Tower of Hanoi (Rs=0.80-0.94) with detailed state-conditional analysis

Technically sound methodology: appropriately handles observation redundancy via embeddings, correctly applies InfoNCE for MI estimation, and provides scalable alternative to classical counting-based estimators
Honest limitations discussion: explicitly identifies failure modes (reasoning bottlenecks in WebArena Shopping, hallucination-induced diversity in τ-bench Retail) rather than obscuring them
Comprehensive experimental scope: evaluates across multiple environment types (textual games, web navigation, tool-use) with extensive ablations and supplementary analysis
Interesting practical application: authentication case study (Figure 9) demonstrates potential for detecting pivotal behaviors without manual annotation
weaknesses: Core hypothesis unreliably validated: empowerment fails to correlate with capability in critical cases—WebArena Shopping shows flat relationship, τ-bench Retail shows inverse correlation (Rs=-0.50) where smaller models with more hallucinations have higher empowerment; overall WebArena correlation is only moderate (Rs=0.39)

Fundamental confound between diversity and competent control: in floor-performance regimes, diverse invalid outputs are indistinguishable from diverse valid control, making the metric unreliable when reasoning (not environment control) is the capability bottleneck

Weak theoretical justification: the lower-bound theorem in A.2 relies on three unvalidated assumptions (uniform reward distribution, ergodicity, Boltzmann rationality) that real tasks violate; provides lower bound on expected reward, not correlation guarantee with empirical performance

Negative empowerment values due to approximation bias: InfoNCE lower bound yields negative MI estimates that violate information-theoretic definitions; interpretation as 'relative empowerment' undermines the grounding in information theory

Inadequate baseline comparisons: only compares to trivial baselines (visitation entropy, action entropy); no comparison to other capability metrics, simpler alternatives (trajectory length, task success), or principled guidance on when empowerment is reliable

Limited practical utility and unclear scope: WebArena correlation too weak for reliable agent ranking; data requirements and costs relative to task-based evaluation are underspecified; no guidance provided on when to trust the metric beyond post-hoc observation

Reproducibility and methodological concerns: code not provided; hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary (Appendix K shows MiniLM-L6-v2 outperforms larger E5-Base-v2 but why is not explained); LoRA configuration not justified

Natural language robustness degraded in complex settings: EELMA-NL performance degrades significantly in Tower of Hanoi (0.223 vs 0.295 for direct estimation), suggesting brittleness to linguistic variation despite claims of robustness

Shallow capability analysis: does not systematically analyze which agent capabilities drive empowerment (reasoning vs environment knowledge); relies on anecdotal case studies rather than principled decomposition
Limited algorithmic novelty: EELMA combines existing components (pretrained embeddings, LoRA, standard InfoNCE) in straightforward ways; novelty limited to application domain rather than methodology

strengths: Addresses timely problem of goal-agnostic LM agent evaluation with clear motivation and practical safety applications
Sound technical contribution: EELMA elegantly adapts empowerment to text via learned embeddings and InfoNCE, handling observation redundancy and linguistic variability effectively
Comprehensive empirical validation: strong correlation with ground truth (Rs=0.80-0.94), robustness testing with NL paraphrasing, broad environment coverage (games, web, tools), extensive ablations
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, prompts, training curves in appendices; code promised; clear computational specs
Honest about limitations: Section 6 identifies failure modes (reasoning bottlenecks, floor performance, task-irrelevant control) without overselling
Practical applications demonstrated: authentication case study shows power-seeking detection without explicit rewards, enabling continuous safety monitoring
Rigorous theoretical foundation: Appendix A properly grounds empowerment in information theory with connection to expected reward under stated assumptions
weaknesses: Gap between theory and practice: Uniform reward assumption (Appendix A.2) is strong; limited characterization of when this holds vs. breaks down in realistic settings

Boundary conditions undermine generality claims: WebArena Shopping shows flat empowerment-reward relationship attributed vaguely to 'reasoning bottleneck'; τ-bench retail shows empowerment inversion at floor performance (Rs=-0.50)—insufficient investigation of these failures

InfoNCE approximation bias not fully characterized: Equation 6 requires Et,o∗[C1(ot,at)−C2(ot)]≈0 for finite K; unclear if C1−C2 is systematically biased in certain environments; negative empowerment values (Appendix G.4) make metric less intuitive
Somewhat incremental over Myers et al. (2024): Main novelty is engineering an estimator for text via embeddings+InfoNCE; no fundamentally new insights about empowerment theory itself
Limited practical guidance: Positioned as 'complementary' metric but provides minimal guidance on when to use empowerment vs. task rewards in practice or how to weight them

Narrow baseline comparisons: Compares mainly to simple diversity metrics (entropy, state coverage); missing comparisons to other goal-agnostic measures from RL literature or other information-theoretic approaches

Incomplete investigation of failure modes: WebArena Shopping domain failure addressed only with post-hoc explanation rather than deeper investigation; τ-bench retail threshold for metric breakdown not thoroughly explored
Cross-domain generalization not tested: No evidence that EELMA transfers across environments (e.g., encoder trained on web tasks to tool-use)
